---
title: On Stoic Virtue and Self-Discipline
lang: en
free: true
---

A synthesis of Stoic teachings from Marcus Aurelius on practical virtue: how to act well, bear difficulty, and remain undisturbed. Drawn from the core Stoic tradition that virtue alone is the good, and that our judgements — not external events — are the source of all disturbance.

## The Governing Principle

The rational, governing faculty of the human being is its most essential part. Marcus calls it the *hegemonikon* — the ruling principle that steers thoughts, judgements, and actions. When it is properly ordered, aligned with nature and reason, a person can meet any circumstance without being upset or deflected. External events neither harm nor benefit the governing mind; they are simply material for it to work upon.

The mind is like a flame. A small, weak fire is extinguished by whatever is thrown at it. But a great and vigorous fire assimilates whatever is cast upon it, burns through it, and grows larger from the very things meant to quench it. This is the aspiration of Stoic practice: cultivate the inner fire until it is strong enough to turn every obstacle into fuel.

## Virtue Is Within Reach

You may say you are not gifted with a keen intelligence. That is no excuse. There is much that lies entirely within your own power: honesty, dignity, endurance, freedom from the desire for pleasure, contentment, kindness, freedom, simplicity, few words, a great spirit. Do you not see how much you could already display — qualities for which no natural incapacity can be pleaded — and yet you voluntarily remain below? Are you forced by inborn weakness to grumble, to be greedy, to flatter, to blame your body, to be obsequious, to boast, to be so restless in your soul? By the gods, you could have been free of all this long ago. Only this one reproach might fairly be made: that you are a man somewhat slow and dull. And even that you must work at, not dismissing it with comfortable excuses.

Show what is entirely in your power. Show virtue: straightforwardness, self-restraint, endurance. Show that you can be free — free from anger, from greed, from fear of death, from anxiety about reputation. These are achievements open to any rational being.

## Acting Without Expectation of Return

One person, having done good to another, immediately sets it down as a debt owed to him. Another does not keep a ledger, but privately still regards the other as a debtor and remembers what he did. But a third person is as if he does not know what he has done: he is like a vine that has borne a cluster of grapes and, having produced its fruit, asks nothing more. A horse runs its race, a dog takes a scent, a bee makes honey — and none of them clamour for praise. Such should a person be who does good: not crying it out, but passing on to the next action, just as a vine passes on to bear another cluster in its season.

## Patience With Imperfection

Do not be disgusted, do not give up, do not lose heart if you do not manage in every instance to act from correct principles. If you are thrown off course, return — and be glad if most of your conduct is worthy of a human being. Return to philosophy not as a schoolboy to a harsh master, but as a sore-eyed person returns to a sponge and egg-white, or another to a poultice, another to a warm lotion. In this way you will not parade your obedience to reason but will find rest in it.

Remember: philosophy desires only what your own nature desires. And you were wishing for something not in accordance with nature. Now ask which is more pleasant — the comfortable yielding to pleasure, or the steady practice of magnanimity, freedom, simplicity, consideration, and piety? For what is more pleasant than the working of wisdom itself — its smooth, uninterrupted movement, understanding what it means to know?

## On What Is Truly Good

As to those things which the majority call goods, consider this test. If a person were to think in advance of the genuine goods — intelligence, self-restraint, justice, courage — then, with those ideas in mind, he could not bear to hear the expression "burdened by good things," for it does not apply. But if he were to think in advance of what the masses call goods — wealth, luxury, fame — then he would readily accept that phrase as apt and clever. This shows that the crowd feels the difference instinctively. One expression grates and is rejected; the other is accepted as a pointed witticism. Ask yourself then: should you honour and count as good things about which, when thought through, the appropriate remark is a comic one?

## Bearing Whatever Falls

It is not given to anyone to suffer what is truly beyond his strength. Whatever falls to another person, he either does not perceive what has happened, or rises above it through the greatness of his soul. It is strange, then, that ignorance and vanity should prove stronger than wisdom.

The good man bears what falls to him willingly, not because he has no feelings, but because he understands that what happens to each of us is part of the fabric of the whole. Just as all bodies together compose the world-body, so all causes compose the single cause we call fate. To resist it angrily is to tear at the fabric of things. To receive it with equanimity is to cooperate with the intelligence that governs all.
